title: Channels & select
scopeHtml: Channel basics, capacities, close vs cancel, produce/pipelines, fan-out/fan-in, select, trySend, Channel vs Flow, and UI-event pitfalls (kotlinx.coroutines 1.7 to 1.10 era).

notes.title: Channel basics
notes.html:
The idea. A Channel is a pipe between coroutines. One side puts values in (send), the other side takes them out (receive). If the pipe is full the sender waits; if it is empty the receiver waits. Waiting means suspending, not blocking a thread.

The mechanism. Channel<T> implements both SendChannel<T> and ReceiveChannel<T>. Each value is delivered to exactly one receiver. Main operations: send, receive, trySend, tryReceive, close, cancel, receiveCatching, iteration with for (x in ch).

val ch = Channel<Int>()
launch { for (i in 1..3) ch.send(i); ch.close() }
for (x in ch) println(x)          // 1 2 3, loop ends when closed

How it differs from neighbours:

  • Deferred<T>: one value, one time. A Channel carries a stream.
  • BlockingQueue: put/take block threads. A Channel suspends coroutines, so thousands of waiting coroutines cost almost nothing.
  • Flow: a cold recipe; each collector re-runs it. A Channel is hot: values exist whether or not anyone receives, and each value goes to one receiver.

Real-world. Chat outboxes (WhatsApp-style send queues), upload worker pools, UI one-shot events, and the internals of channelFlow, callbackFlow, buffer(), flowOn, produceIn all sit on Channels.

Everyday analogy. A conveyor belt in a sushi shop. The chef places plates, the customer takes one; each plate is eaten by exactly one person.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking a Channel broadcasts to all receivers (it does not; that is SharedFlow).
  • Forgetting the channel is hot: sent values wait in the buffer even with no receiver.
  • Comparing it to BlockingQueue and forgetting the suspension vs thread-blocking difference.

notes.title: Channel capacities
notes.html:
The idea. Capacity says how many items the pipe can hold before the sender must wait.

Capacity Buffer send suspends when Notes
RENDEZVOUS (0, default) none no receiver is waiting sender and receiver meet; strongest back-pressure
BUFFERED 64 by default (system property kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer) buffer full used by buffer()
N (e.g. 10) N buffer full explicit size
CONFLATED 1, keeps only the latest never new value overwrites unreceived old one
UNLIMITED grows without limit (linked segments) never can OOM

Picking. RENDEZVOUS for strict hand-off and when you want the producer to be slowed by the consumer. BUFFERED/N for smoothing small bursts. CONFLATED for "only the latest matters" (progress, sensor value for a UI), accepting lost values. UNLIMITED only when the producer is provably bounded or the consumer provably fast; otherwise it hides a memory leak.

val progress = Channel<Int>(Channel.CONFLATED)
val queue    = Channel<Job>(capacity = 100)
val events   = Channel<UiEvent>(Channel.BUFFERED)

Real-world. Wearable and fitness apps (Fitbit-style) streaming 100 Hz sensor samples that used UNLIMITED and a slow DB writer saw the OOM-kill rate climb. The sensible design: a bounded buffer plus batching, or CONFLATED for the live chart and a separate bounded queue for persistence.

Everyday analogy. RENDEZVOUS is handing a parcel hand-to-hand. A buffer is a mailbox that holds 64 letters. CONFLATED is a whiteboard where only the latest note is kept.

Common interview traps.

  • Using UNLIMITED "to avoid suspension" and getting a memory growth incident.
  • Expecting CONFLATED to deliver every item.
  • Not knowing that Channel() defaults to RENDEZVOUS.

notes.title: Suspension semantics of send and receive
notes.html:
The idea. Who waits for whom depends on capacity.

  • RENDEZVOUS: send suspends until a receiver arrives; receive suspends until a sender arrives. They meet.
  • Buffered N: send suspends only when N items are waiting; receive suspends only when the buffer is empty.
  • CONFLATED / UNLIMITED: send never suspends. receive suspends when empty.

Fairness. Channels are fair: waiting senders and waiting receivers are served in FIFO order. If three coroutines call receive, the first to arrive gets the first element. A stream is not "stolen" by a lucky later receiver.

Cancellation. A suspended send/receive is cancellable. If the sender is cancelled while suspended, the element is not added (for rendezvous/full buffer it never entered). But there is a gap: if the element was already handed over and the receiver is cancelled before it resumes, the element can be lost; that is what onUndeliveredElement is for.

RENDEZVOUS timeline
sender:   send(1) ...suspended........... resumes
receiver:               receive() arrives ^ gets 1

Real-world. In a worker pool, 4 workers each looping on receive on a rendezvous channel get jobs in FIFO fairness, a natural round-robin.

Everyday analogy. A deli counter with a numbered ticket system. Customers (receivers) are served in ticket order, not by who shouts loudest.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing send on a BUFFERED channel always suspends or never suspends (it depends on fullness).
  • Ignoring that cancelling a coroutine may drop an in-flight element without onUndeliveredElement.
  • Confusing "fair" with "each receiver gets equal work" (it is FIFO order of waiting, not equal totals).

notes.title: close versus cancel and iteration
notes.html:
The idea. close() says "no more items are coming; deliver what is queued and then stop". cancel() says "throw everything away and stop now".

The mechanism.

  • SendChannel.close(cause?): marks the end. Already buffered items are still received. Then receive throws ClosedReceiveChannelException (or cause if you passed one), for loops end normally, receiveCatching returns a closed result. send after close throws ClosedSendChannelException (or cause).
  • ReceiveChannel.cancel(cause?): closes the channel and drops all buffered elements (calling onUndeliveredElement for them). Pending receive and send fail with CancellationException. cancel is the consumer saying "I'm leaving".
  • for (x in channel) ends when the channel is closed and drained. If nobody ever closes it, the loop never ends and the coroutine leaks.
val ch = Channel<Int>(3)
ch.send(1); ch.send(2)
ch.close()
println(ch.receive())          // 1  (buffered items survive close)
println(ch.receive())          // 2
runCatching { ch.receive() }   // ClosedReceiveChannelException

Scenario: importer never finishes. A batch importer launches a producer that sends 500 rows, then for (row in channel) in the consumer. All rows process but the dialog never dismisses and one coroutine leaks per import. Cause: the producer never calls close(), so the consumer waits forever for row 501. Fix: try { ... } finally { channel.close() } in the producer, or use produce { } which closes automatically.

Real-world. Use close() for the "end of stream" signal from a producer; use cancel() in a consumer's finally/onCompletion, so an abandoned consumer frees the producer.

Everyday analogy. close() is the shop hanging a "last orders" sign: customers already inside are still served. cancel() is a fire alarm: everyone out, food discarded.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to close, hanging every for consumer.
  • Thinking close() discards buffered items (it does not).
  • Calling send after another coroutine closed the channel and crashing with ClosedSendChannelException.

notes.title: produce, consumeEach and pipelines
notes.html:
The idea. produce is "launch a coroutine whose output is a channel", and it closes the channel for you. consumeEach is "loop over this channel and cancel it when I'm done or fail".

The mechanism.

fun CoroutineScope.numbers(): ReceiveChannel<Int> = produce {
    var x = 1
    while (true) send(x++)
}
fun CoroutineScope.square(src: ReceiveChannel<Int>): ReceiveChannel<Int> = produce {
    for (x in src) send(x * x)
}
val result = square(numbers())
repeat(5) { println(result.receive()) }
coroutineContext.cancelChildren()      // stop the pipeline

Lifecycle rules:

  • produce returns a ReceiveChannel, runs as a child of the scope it is called on, and closes the channel when the block finishes (normally or with an exception, which closes with that cause).
  • If the consumer stops early, you must cancel() the channel (or cancel the scope), otherwise the producer stays suspended in send forever (a leak).
  • consumeEach { } iterates and cancels the channel at the end or on failure, so it can be used only once, and it kills fan-out to other consumers when one consumer finishes.
  • Pipelines are an extension on CoroutineScope so that structured concurrency owns the stages. produce is @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi in older versions; check your version.

Real-world. Log/event processing pipelines (read -> parse -> upload), image processing stages (decode -> resize -> encode) and Flow operators like flowOn use this shape internally.

Everyday analogy. An assembly line: each station takes from the previous belt and puts onto the next. When the first belt runs out and is shut, each station shuts its own belt in turn.

Common interview traps.

  • Leaving a pipeline running after the screen is gone (no cancel of the scope).
  • Using consumeEach and then trying to receive again (channel already cancelled).
  • Creating a pipeline stage outside a CoroutineScope, losing structured concurrency.

notes.title: Fan-out and fan-in
notes.html:
The idea. Fan-out: many consumers read from one channel and each element goes to just one of them (work sharing). Fan-in: many producers send into one channel.

The mechanism.

fun CoroutineScope.worker(id: Int, jobs: ReceiveChannel<Job>, results: SendChannel<Result>) =
    launch { for (job in jobs) results.send(process(job)) }

val jobs = Channel<Job>(); val results = Channel<Result>(10)
coroutineScope {
    repeat(4) { worker(it, jobs, results) }
    // producer sends, then jobs.close()
}

Distribution is FIFO-fair among waiting workers, so work goes to whichever is idle. Use for loops, not consumeEach, in workers: consumeEach cancels the shared channel when one worker ends, killing the others. Clean shutdown: the producer close()s the jobs channel; workers drain and exit; after all workers finish, close the results channel (e.g. a parent coroutine joins the workers and then closes it).

Failure handling in pools. A photo backup with 4 workers stalls at 40% with the notification still showing "running": one worker throws an unhandled exception for a bad file, cancels the scope... or, if workers were launched inside a supervisorScope/own scope, just that worker dies. The remaining workers keep going, but when all die the queue is no longer drained and send suspends forever. Defensive design: try/catch per job inside the worker so a bad item becomes a recorded failure, use runCatching that does not swallow CancellationException, and report results explicitly.

Real-world. Upload services, thumbnail generators and sync engines use a fixed number of workers over a channel (a simple, bounded alternative to a Semaphore).

Everyday analogy. Several cashiers serving one queue of customers: each customer goes to whichever cashier is free.

Common interview traps.

  • consumeEach in each worker closing the shared channel.
  • A worker crash silently stopping the pipeline.
  • Expecting results in input order (parallel workers finish out of order).

notes.title: onBufferOverflow and onUndeliveredElement
notes.html:
The idea. onBufferOverflow decides what happens when the buffer is full. onUndeliveredElement is a cleanup hook for elements that were sent but never reached a consumer.

onBufferOverflow (a BufferOverflow value in Channel(capacity, onBufferOverflow)):

  • SUSPEND (default): send waits.
  • DROP_OLDEST: remove the oldest buffered item, keep the new one.
  • DROP_LATEST: ignore the new item. Only meaningful with a buffer ≥ 1; CONFLATED is just capacity 1 with DROP_OLDEST. The unlimited and rendezvous capacities do not accept a non-default overflow.

onUndeliveredElement. Called when a sent element is dropped: channel cancelled with items in the buffer, a send that was cancelled after hand-over, a DROP_* overflow, or trySend on a closed channel. Needed when elements own resources (a Bitmap, a Closeable, a file handle, a lease) and must be released.

val ch = Channel<Bitmap>(
    capacity = 8,
    onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST,
    onUndeliveredElement = { it.recycle() }       // must not throw; runs on whatever thread dropped it
)

The handler should be fast, must not throw (exceptions are reported as UndeliveredElementException), and must not touch the channel.

Real-world. Camera frame streams (CameraX ImageProxy must be close()d) use a drop-oldest policy plus cleanup; otherwise the camera stalls after its small image pool is exhausted.

Everyday analogy. A full coat-check: either the new guest waits (SUSPEND), the oldest coat is thrown away (DROP_OLDEST), or the new coat is refused (DROP_LATEST). The cleanup hook is the person who returns the dropped coat's token.

Common interview traps.

  • Using DROP_* and leaking resources held by dropped items.
  • Throwing from onUndeliveredElement.
  • Expecting the handler to run only for cancelled receivers (it also runs on overflow drops).

notes.title: trySend, trySendBlocking and tryReceive
notes.html:
The idea. Regular send can suspend, but some code is not allowed to suspend (a plain Java callback, a onSensorChanged). The try* functions never suspend.

The mechanism. trySend(e) returns a ChannelResult<Unit> immediately: success, failed (buffer full), or closed. tryReceive() returns a ChannelResult<T>. trySendBlocking(e) (in kotlinx.coroutines.channels) blocks the thread until it can send, so only use it on a thread that may block (not Main).

val r = ch.trySend(value)
if (r.isFailure) { /* full or closed: drop, log, or fall back */ }
r.isClosed          // true if closed
r.exceptionOrNull() // the close cause

Use trySend in callbacks with a CONFLATED/DROP_OLDEST/large buffer where dropping is acceptable. Use trySendBlocking in a callback on a dedicated background thread when loss is unacceptable and the buffer is bounded. Inside a coroutine, prefer send.

Real-world. callbackFlow bodies use trySend from sensor, location and Firebase listeners; Google's own docs and many samples do the same.

Everyday analogy. trySend is dropping a letter in the box and walking away if it is full. trySendBlocking is standing at the box till there is room.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring the ChannelResult and silently losing events.
  • Calling trySendBlocking on the main thread (ANR risk).
  • Using trySend on a rendezvous channel with no receiver ready (it fails).

notes.title: select expression
notes.html:
The idea. select waits on several possible events and takes whichever happens first, like Promise.race for channels, timeouts and Deferreds.

The mechanism. Clauses: ch.onReceive, ch.onReceiveCatching, ch.onSend(value), deferred.onAwait, job.onJoin, onTimeout(ms) (experimental, check your version).

suspend fun next(a: ReceiveChannel<String>, b: ReceiveChannel<String>): String =
    select {
        a.onReceive { "A:$it" }
        b.onReceive { "B:$it" }
        onTimeout(500) { "timeout" }
    }

Which wins if several are ready? select is biased to the first clause in source order. If a always has data, b is never picked. selectUnbiased { } randomizes the order. onReceive on a closed channel throws; use onReceiveCatching to handle closing.

Internals and guarantees. select registers one SelectInstance on every clause's channel/deferred. The first event that wins a CAS on the instance's state "selects" it; all other registrations are then unregistered (cleanup cost is O(clauses) per call). So exactly one clause fires, and a value is only taken from the winning channel. The cost: allocation of the select object and clause registrations on every loop iteration, so avoid it in very hot paths. Danger: a clause onSend(compute()) evaluates its value expression before the select decides, so side effects in that expression run even for clauses that lose; compute pure values only and perform side effects inside the clause's result lambda. A correct "priority queue with timeout": first tryReceive on critical, then tryReceive on normal, and only if both are empty use a select with onReceiveCatching on both plus onTimeout, so priority is explicit and the select only handles waiting.

Starvation incident. A notification service with critical, normal, bulk channels in one biased select was designed with critical first. Under a flood of critical items, normal and bulk starved; the reverse bug (bulk first) delays alerts. Fixes: bounded fairness (after N critical items, poll other channels with tryReceive), selectUnbiased, or separate consumers with separate dispatchers.

Real-world. Multiplexing a data channel and a "stop"/"refresh" channel, request-with-timeout, hedged requests to two servers.

Everyday analogy. Waiting at a restaurant for either the soup or the salad: you eat whichever arrives first, and if both arrive together the waiter always serves the first-listed.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming random fairness when several channels are ready.
  • Not handling closed channels (exception from onReceive).
  • Treating onTimeout as stable API without checking the version.

notes.title: Channel versus Flow
notes.html:
The idea. A Flow is a description of a stream; a Channel is a live queue.

Question Choose
Each subscriber should get its own run of the producer Flow (cold)
Work items consumed by exactly one worker Channel
Need operators (map, combine, debounce) Flow
Hand-off between long-lived coroutines, queue semantics, back-pressure, workers Channel
State the UI observes (latest value, replay) StateFlow
Event multicast to many SharedFlow
One-shot UI events that must not be lost Channel with care (see below) or state-based events

Rule: expose a Flow at API boundaries (it is cancel-safe and composable), and use a Channel inside when you need queue/actor semantics. callbackFlow/channelFlow give you a Flow whose implementation uses a Channel.

UI events and Channels. A ViewModel sending "navigate to confirmation" through a Channel consumed with receiveAsFlow() while collecting in repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) works until the screen is stopped at the wrong moment: if the collector is cancelled while the item is being delivered, the event can be lost ("paid, nothing happened"), and with no collector the event waits in the buffer and is delivered later, possibly twice after config change patterns. Production symptom: no crash, support tickets ("charged but still on payment screen") and low-end devices on Android 9 to 11 with aggressive background kill make it likelier. Robust approach: model the event as state that the UI consumes and clears (events: List<Event> in UiState, with onEventHandled(id)), as recommended by Google's architecture guidance; or at least onUndeliveredElement plus careful lifecycle.

Real-world. Android's guidance moved from SingleLiveEvent to state-based events for this reason.

Everyday analogy. A Flow is a TV channel recording you can replay from the start; a Channel is a single parcel passed to one person and gone.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "Flow is more modern". Give criteria: cold vs hot, one consumer vs many, operators.
  • Believing a Channel for UI events is lossless.
  • Forgetting that two collectors of a receiveAsFlow() split items.

notes.title: receiveAsFlow versus consumeAsFlow
notes.html:
The idea. Both turn a channel into a Flow. They differ in what happens at the end and with multiple collectors.

receiveAsFlow() consumeAsFlow()
Collectors can be collected multiple times / concurrently; each element goes to one of them (fan-out) only once; collecting twice throws IllegalStateException
When a collector is cancelled channel stays open channel is cancelled (consumed)
Typical use events consumed across screen restarts/lifecycle one-shot stream that dies with its collector

So for a ViewModel's event channel observed from a UI that is repeatedly started and stopped (repeatOnLifecycle), consumeAsFlow() would permanently kill the channel on the first stop; receiveAsFlow() keeps it alive. With two collectors (say two fragments) on receiveAsFlow(), each event goes to only one, never both.

Real-world. receiveAsFlow() is the common pattern in ViewModels for one-shot events (Compose LaunchedEffect + viewModel.events.collect).

Everyday analogy. receiveAsFlow is a pickup counter anyone can step up to. consumeAsFlow is a locked mailbox that shreds the contents when the owner leaves.

Common interview traps.

  • Using consumeAsFlow with lifecycle-aware collection and losing all events after the first stop.
  • Collecting the same receiveAsFlow in two places and expecting both to see each event.
  • Not remembering that cancelling a receiveAsFlow collector can still drop an in-flight element.

notes.title: Channel as a queue and the outbox pattern
notes.html:
The idea. When tasks must happen in order, one at a time, and never twice, a Channel with a single consumer is a natural queue (an actor).

Design for a chat outbox. Messages sent offline must be delivered in order per conversation, retried with backoff, never double-sent. Today scope.launch { api.send(msg) } per message lets sends overlap and reorder. Better:

private val queues = ConcurrentHashMap<ConversationId, Channel<Message>>()

fun enqueue(m: Message) {
    val ch = queues.computeIfAbsent(m.conversationId) { id ->
        Channel<Message>(Channel.UNLIMITED).also { c -> scope.launch { drain(c) } }
    }
    ch.trySend(m)
}
private suspend fun drain(c: ReceiveChannel<Message>) {
    for (m in c) retryWithBackoff { api.send(m, idempotencyKey = m.localId) }
}

Key points: one consumer per conversation preserves order; an idempotency key (client-generated id) makes retries safe; persist the queue (Room) because a Channel does not survive process death, then let WorkManager resume sending; bound or persist rather than UNLIMITED in memory. Idle queues need clean-up (close and remove from the map).

Real-world. WhatsApp/Telegram outboxes and Gmail's "Outbox" folder store pending items durably and drain with retries.

Everyday analogy. One post-office clerk per street, processing letters in the order they arrive.

Common interview traps.

  • Using an in-memory Channel as the only copy of pending data (lost on process death).
  • Retrying without an idempotency key (double sends).
  • Letting one failing message block the whole queue forever without a poison-message policy.

notes.title: Channel internals and obsolete APIs
notes.html:
The idea. A modern Channel is a lock-free queue made of linked segments, with cells that hold either an element or a waiting coroutine.

Internals (approximate, confirm in source). Since kotlinx.coroutines 1.7 (the rewrite based on the paper "Fast and Scalable Channels in Kotlin Coroutines"), the channel uses atomic counters for senders/receivers and an infinite array emulated by segments; a send and a receive rendezvous in a cell. Older versions used a linked list with CAS plus a lock for the buffered variant. For the interview: it is non-blocking, fair, and cheap per operation; waiting coroutines are stored as continuations in cells.

Obsolete/removed APIs and replacements.

Old Status Replacement
BroadcastChannel deprecated, moving to removal SharedFlow
ConflatedBroadcastChannel deprecated StateFlow
actor { } obsolete (delicate) own Channel + launch
receiveOrNull() removed/deprecated receiveCatching()
offer() removed trySend()
poll() removed tryReceive()

Scenario: fan-out used as broadcast. A ride-hailing LocationRepository exposes a ReceiveChannel<Location> and both the map screen and ETA service loop over it. Each location goes to only one of them, so the map "jitters" and the ETA is off (each sees every second point). Fix: expose a SharedFlow/StateFlow (broadcast to all) via shareIn/stateIn, not a shared channel.

Everyday analogy. The channel is a library return trolley with numbered shelves; the arrays of shelves get added as needed.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a ReceiveChannel property as a multicast.
  • Citing offer, poll, receiveOrNull as current APIs.
  • Quoting internals with false certainty. Say "confirm in the source for your version".

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A Channel is a hot, fair, suspending queue; each element goes to exactly one receiver.
  • Default capacity is RENDEZVOUS (0); BUFFERED is 64; CONFLATED keeps latest; UNLIMITED can OOM.
  • close() lets buffered items drain, cancel() drops them; a for loop only ends when closed.
  • produce closes for you; use for (not consumeEach) in fan-out workers; handle per-job failures.
  • onBufferOverflow picks the drop policy; onUndeliveredElement frees resources of dropped items.
  • trySend for non-suspending callbacks, trySendBlocking only off the main thread.
  • select is biased to the first ready clause; starvation needs explicit fairness.
  • Flow for composable cold streams, Channel for queues/hand-off; UI events are safer as state.
  • receiveAsFlow survives collector cancellation; consumeAsFlow kills the channel.
  • Persist outboxes; use idempotency keys; replace BroadcastChannel/actor with SharedFlow/Channel.

questions.promptHtml: What is a Channel in Kotlin coroutines, how is it different from a Deferred or a plain BlockingQueue, and what are the main operations?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you see Channel as a coroutine-aware communication primitive (suspension instead of blocking) and not "a queue".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Channel is a hot, non-blocking queue between coroutines. send suspends when the channel cannot take the element, receive suspends when it is empty, so nothing blocks a thread. Unlike a Deferred, which carries exactly one value, a Channel carries a stream of values. Unlike a BlockingQueue, waiting costs a suspended continuation instead of a parked thread. It is split into SendChannel and ReceiveChannel so I can hand out only the half each side needs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A channel solves the producer/consumer problem between coroutines that may run on different threads. The interface is the union of two halves:

Channel<E> : SendChannel<E>, ReceiveChannel<E>

SendChannel<E>:    send(e) [suspend]  trySend(e)  close(cause?)  invokeOnClose{}  onSend (select)
ReceiveChannel<E>: receive() [suspend]  receiveCatching() [suspend]  tryReceive()
                   iterator()  cancel(cause?)  onReceive / onReceiveCatching (select)

Key properties:

  • Hot: elements exist independent of any collector. Producing starts when someone calls send, not when someone receives.
  • Each element is delivered to exactly one receiver (point-to-point, not broadcast). Two coroutines calling receive split the stream between them.
  • Fair: suspended senders and receivers are resumed in FIFO order.
  • Thread-safe: any number of senders and receivers on any dispatchers can use one channel.
  • Backpressure by suspension: how much a sender can run ahead is the channel capacity (Q449).

Versus others:

Channel Deferred BlockingQueue
Values 0..N, then close exactly 1 0..N
Waiting suspends suspends (await) blocks thread
Delivery one receiver per element many awaiters see same value one consumer per element
Cancellation aware yes yes only via interrupt

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.*

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val ch = Channel<Int>()              // RENDEZVOUS by default
    launch {
        for (i in 1..3) ch.send(i)       // suspends until receiver is ready
        ch.close()                       // tell the consumer "no more"
    }
    for (x in ch) println(x)             // loop ends when channel is closed and drained
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting close(): a for (x in ch) consumer waits forever (see Q455).
  • Assuming a channel is broadcast. Two consumers each get a subset of the elements.
  • Exposing the full Channel publicly so outsiders can send/close; expose ReceiveChannel or a Flow.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a Channel hot or cold? → Hot. It holds state (buffer, waiters) regardless of consumers; contrast with flow {} which re-runs per collector.
  2. Is it thread-safe? → Yes, send/receive are safe from any number of coroutines on any threads; fairness is FIFO.
  3. Why not just use ConcurrentLinkedQueue? → No suspension, so you would poll or block a thread; no close semantics, no cancellation propagation, no backpressure.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE answer says "it is like a queue between coroutines". Senior adds: exactly-once point-to-point delivery, FIFO fairness, suspension-based backpressure, the Send/Receive split for API design, and that most application code should wrap it in a Flow instead of exposing it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that exposed a raw Channel from a repository had unrelated callers calling close() on it, killing event delivery for everyone until restart.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the Channel capacity options RENDEZVOUS, BUFFERED, CONFLATED, UNLIMITED and a custom number. What is the default and when would you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Capacity is the whole backpressure and data-loss story of a channel. Wrong capacity is the root cause of most Channel bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Channel() with no argument is RENDEZVOUS, capacity 0: sender and receiver must meet. BUFFERED is a fixed buffer, default 64 (changeable by the kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer system property). CONFLATED keeps only the latest element and never suspends the sender. UNLIMITED never suspends the sender and grows without bound, so it can OOM. A positive number gives that exact buffer size. I pick based on whether I want backpressure (RENDEZVOUS or sized), latest-wins (CONFLATED), or never-block-and-I-accept-the-memory-risk (UNLIMITED).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Capacity Buffer send suspends when Drops? Typical use
RENDEZVOUS (0, default) none no receiver waiting no strict handoff, lock-step pipelines
n > 0 n buffer full no (SUSPEND) decouple bursty producer from slower consumer
BUFFERED 64 default buffer full no "reasonable default buffer"
CONFLATED 1 never yes, oldest replaced "latest state wins" (progress, position)
UNLIMITED growable never no must never block sender; bounded by your own discipline

Details worth knowing:

  • CONFLATED is equivalent to capacity 1 with BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST. BUFFERED interacts with onBufferOverflow: with SUSPEND it is 64; if you pick DROP_* with BUFFERED, the buffer is still the default size.
  • With RENDEZVOUS plus DROP_OLDEST/DROP_LATEST, the factory creates a buffer of 1 (a rendezvous cannot drop anything). I treat the exact corner-case mapping as "check the KDoc" rather than rely on memory. CONFLATED and UNLIMITED combined with a non-SUSPEND overflow throw IllegalArgumentException.
  • Any other negative number throws IllegalArgumentException.
  • Memory for a large positive capacity is allocated lazily, so Channel(10_000) does not allocate 10k slots up front.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val handoff  = Channel<Job>()                                  // RENDEZVOUS
val buffered = Channel<Job>(Channel.BUFFERED)                  // 64 by default
val latest   = Channel<Progress>(Channel.CONFLATED)            // keep newest only
val lossy    = Channel<Tick>(capacity = 16, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)
val unbounded = Channel<LogLine>(Channel.UNLIMITED)            // OOM risk, see Q463

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using UNLIMITED "to avoid suspension bugs" and trading a visible hang for a silent OOM.
  • Using CONFLATED for events that must all be handled (a click, a payment result) and silently dropping some.
  • Believing BUFFERED is unlimited; it is 64.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does Channel<Int>(0) do vs Channel<Int>()? → Same: RENDEZVOUS.
  2. How do you make a channel drop the newest instead of the oldest? → onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST with a positive capacity.
  3. Why can CONFLATED never suspend the sender but still be "lossless" for state? → Because only the latest state matters; each new value supersedes the last, same idea as StateFlow conflation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists the four names. Senior: states 64 and the system property, explains the overflow-strategy pairing rules, maps each capacity to a failure mode (hang, drop, OOM) and ties choice to the data semantics (events vs state).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A telemetry channel set to UNLIMITED filled to hundreds of MB during a network outage on low-RAM devices and caused OOM kills.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through exactly when send and receive suspend for each capacity. What does "fair" mean and what happens when a suspended send is cancelled?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests mental model of runtime behavior, which is what you need to debug "my producer is stuck" or "my element vanished".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: receive suspends when the buffer is empty and no sender is waiting. send suspends when there is no room: on RENDEZVOUS that means no receiver is waiting; on a sized buffer it means the buffer is full. UNLIMITED and CONFLATED never suspend send. Waiting parties are queued FIFO, so channels are fair. If a suspended send is cancelled, that element is not delivered, and onUndeliveredElement fires if I configured it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Think of three states of a channel with capacity n:

empty buffer, receivers waiting     -> send hands element straight to first waiting receiver (no buffering)
buffer has room                     -> send stores element, returns immediately
buffer full / no receiver (n=0)     -> send parks continuation in the sender queue

and symmetrically for receive:

buffer has element                  -> receive takes it; if a sender is parked, its element moves into buffer and it resumes
buffer empty, senders parked (n=0)  -> receive takes directly from the first parked sender
buffer empty, no senders            -> receive parks

Fairness: parked senders and receivers are resumed in arrival order. It does not mean threads alternate; it means no starvation of an earlier waiter by a later one.

Cancellation: send and receive are cancellable suspension points. Cancelling a parked send removes it from the queue; the element was never delivered. There is a subtle window: if the element was already handed to a receiver whose coroutine is cancelled before it resumes, the element is also undelivered. The doc'd contract: onUndeliveredElement is invoked for exactly these cases, so resources inside elements (Bitmaps, file handles, sockets) can be closed.

Dispatching note: after receive resumes, the continuation is dispatched on the receiver's own dispatcher, not the sender's. A hand-off is therefore also a thread hop if dispatchers differ.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val ch = Channel<String>()                 // rendezvous
val sender = launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
    println("sending"); ch.send("A")       // parks until someone receives
    println("sent")                        // prints only after receive arrives
}
delay(100)
println(ch.receive())                      // resumes sender

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming send returning means the consumer processed the element. On a buffered channel it only means "enqueued".
  • Assuming strict global ordering across multiple senders. Order is FIFO per arrival at the channel, not per sender launch order.
  • Ignoring that onUndeliveredElement runs in an arbitrary context and must not throw or block.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does send on a CONFLATED channel ever suspend? → No, it replaces the buffered element.
  2. Is receive cancellation-safe? → Yes; the element is either received or stays in the channel, except in the resume-race window covered by onUndeliveredElement.
  3. How would you make a send that gives up after 200 ms? → withTimeoutOrNull(200) { ch.send(x) }; element is undelivered on timeout, so handle it (and see the resource pitfall in the timeout chunk).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "send suspends when full". Senior: draws the three states, knows direct hand-off bypasses the buffer, FIFO fairness, the dispatcher hop on resume, and the undelivered-element window.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An upload queue "lost" frames only under cancellation; the cause was elements in flight to a cancelled receiver, fixed with onUndeliveredElement returning buffers to a pool.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between close() on a SendChannel and cancel() on a ReceiveChannel? What exceptions do send and receive throw afterward, and how does for (x in channel) end?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Lifecycle of a channel is a classic source of hangs and lost data.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: close() is a graceful end-of-stream: no more sends, but receivers still drain what is buffered, then iteration ends. cancel() is abandonment: it closes the channel and discards buffered elements. After close, send throws ClosedSendChannelException; receive on a closed and drained channel throws ClosedReceiveChannelException unless the channel was closed with a cause, in which case that cause is thrown. A for loop ends normally on a plain close and throws the cause if closed with one.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Operation Called on Buffered elements Pending receive New send
close() SendChannel (producer side) kept, still receivable resumes with elements, then closed ClosedSendChannelException (or the cause)
close(cause) SendChannel kept after drain, throws cause throws cause
cancel() ReceiveChannel (consumer side) dropped (onUndeliveredElement called) throws CancellationException throws CancellationException
  • close is idempotent: returns true the first time, false after. invokeOnClose { } lets you register a single handler.
  • receiveCatching() returns a ChannelResult and never throws on close: use isClosed, getOrNull(), exceptionOrNull(). It is the replacement for the removed receiveOrNull.
  • isClosedForSend and isClosedForReceive are marked delicate API: the answer can be stale the instant you read it, so do not use them for control flow.
  • The for loop calls iterator().hasNext(), which suspends until an element arrives or the channel is closed; it returns false after a plain close and drain.
  • cancel is how a consumer says "I do not want any more, stop producing". A producer parked in send then fails with CancellationException, which unwinds it cleanly (Q452 produce ties this to the producer coroutine).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val ch = Channel<Int>(Channel.BUFFERED)
ch.trySend(1); ch.trySend(2)
ch.close()                               // graceful
println(ch.receive())                    // 1
println(ch.receive())                    // 2
println(ch.receiveCatching().isClosed)   // true, no exception
// ch.receive()                          // would throw ClosedReceiveChannelException

val ch2 = Channel<Int>(Channel.BUFFERED)
ch2.trySend(1)
ch2.cancel()                             // buffered 1 is discarded

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Never closing: consumers hang (Q455).
  • Closing from the wrong place when there are several producers: the first one to finish closes the channel while others still send, hitting ClosedSendChannelException.
  • Calling cancel() on the channel from one fan-out worker and killing the other workers (Q453).
  • Catching Exception around receive and swallowing CancellationException.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who should close, the producer or consumer? → Producer closes (end of data); consumer cancels (no longer interested).
  2. How do you propagate a failure to consumers? → close(cause); the consumer's loop throws it after draining buffered items.
  3. Why is isClosedForReceive discouraged? → Check-then-act race; use receiveCatching.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "close ends it". Senior distinguishes graceful vs destructive, the cause propagation, idempotency, receiveCatching, and who owns each call.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A pipeline closed by the first of three producers dropped the other two's data with ClosedSendChannelException only on slow networks.

questions.promptHtml: What do the produce builder and consumeEach give you over manually creating a Channel, and how do you build a pipeline of stages with them? What are the lifecycle rules?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows if you know the structured-concurrency version of channels: producer coroutine owns the channel and closes it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: produce launches a coroutine and returns a ReceiveChannel. The channel is closed automatically when the producer block finishes, and cancelled if it fails or its scope is cancelled. A pipeline is a chain where each stage is a produce that consumes the previous stage's channel. consumeEach iterates and then cancels the channel when done or on exception, which makes it the right terminal consumer for a single-consumer channel but a trap for fan-out.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
produce<E>(context, capacity) { send(...) } is an extension on CoroutineScope, so the producer is a child of the calling scope: if the scope cancels, the producer cancels and the channel is cancelled. Inside the block you are a ProducerScope, which is both a CoroutineScope and a SendChannel; use awaitClose { } when the producer wraps a callback and must clean up. Historically produce carried an experimental opt-in (@ExperimentalCoroutinesApi); check your version's KDoc before relying on it in library code.

Pipeline shape:

numbers() --Channel--> square() --Channel--> filterEven() --Channel--> consumer
 (produce)               (produce)              (produce)

Each stage is a coroutine, so stages run concurrently (stage 2 handles item 1 while stage 1 produces item 2). Backpressure flows backward automatically: if the consumer slows down, the last channel fills, stage 3 parks in send, stage 3 stops receiving, and so on up to the source.

Cancel the scope and the entire pipeline unwinds because every stage is a child.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun CoroutineScope.numbers(): ReceiveChannel<Int> = produce {
    var n = 1
    while (true) send(n++)              // suspends when consumer is slow; cancel-safe
}

fun CoroutineScope.square(src: ReceiveChannel<Int>): ReceiveChannel<Int> = produce {
    for (x in src) send(x * x)
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val out = square(numbers())
    repeat(5) { println(out.receive()) }
    coroutineContext.cancelChildren()   // cancels all stages (a plain 'return' would hang runBlocking)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning a ReceiveChannel from a function that is not a CoroutineScope extension and launching with GlobalScope. The producer leaks.
  • Using consumeEach in several workers on one channel (first to finish cancels the channel for everybody).
  • Forgetting that an infinite producer keeps the parent scope alive; runBlocking never returns.
  • Pipelines per element often cost more in context switches than a plain map; use them for real I/O stages.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if a stage throws? → The exception cancels the produce coroutine and its channel, and (without a supervisor) the parent scope; downstream receivers see cancellation.
  2. How do you stop a pipeline from the consumer side? → Cancel the final channel or the scope; upstream stages parked in send get cancelled via structured concurrency.
  3. When would you use Flow instead? → For cold, operator-rich, single-collector streams; the same pipeline is just flow { }.map{}.filter{} with less ceremony (Q458).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "produce returns a channel". Senior: scope-extension convention, auto-close/cancel rules, awaitClose, backpressure propagation upstream, consumeEach cancel-on-exit trap, and knows Flow usually replaces hand-built pipelines.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An image-processing pipeline using GlobalScope.produce kept decoding after the screen was gone, burning battery and memory.

questions.promptHtml: Explain fan-out and fan-in with channels. How is work distributed, how do you shut it down cleanly, and what are the pitfalls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the standard "worker pool" pattern. Interviewers check distribution semantics and shutdown correctness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Fan-out is several consumers receiving from one channel; each element goes to exactly one of them, so you get a worker pool. Fan-in is several producers sending into one channel. Distribution is FIFO-fair among waiting receivers, roughly round-robin but not guaranteed. For shutdown the producer closes the channel, workers use a plain for loop (not consumeEach), and the scope waits for all workers. For fan-in someone must close the channel only after all producers finish.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Fan-out:   producer ---> [ channel ] ---> worker1
                                     \--> worker2     each element goes to ONE worker
                                      \-> worker3

Fan-in:    producerA \
           producerB  ---> [ channel ] ---> consumer   consumer sees interleaved stream
           producerC /

Fan-out notes:

  • Because receivers are queued FIFO, an idle pool gets items roughly round-robin. A slow item keeps one worker busy while others take the next items: natural load balancing.
  • Ordering across workers is lost. If you need per-key ordering, shard by key into N channels or use one worker per key.
  • Use for (x in ch) in workers. consumeEach cancels the channel when that worker's loop exits (including by exception), which would also kill the other workers.
  • When producer closes the channel, every worker's for ends and the scope completes.

Fan-in notes:

  • Close only after all producers are done: coroutineScope { producers.joinAll(); ch.close() }, or wrap producers in a coroutineScope and close after it returns.
  • Interleaving is by arrival; no ordering between producers.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun processAll(jobs: List<Job>, workers: Int = 4) = coroutineScope {
    val ch = Channel<Job>(Channel.BUFFERED)
    launch { jobs.forEach { ch.send(it) }; ch.close() }          // producer closes
    repeat(workers) { id ->
        launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
            for (job in ch) handle(id, job)                      // plain for, NOT consumeEach
        }
    }
}   // returns when producer and all workers are done

// Fan-in
suspend fun merge(a: ReceiveChannel<Int>, b: ReceiveChannel<Int>): ReceiveChannel<Int> = coroutineScope {
    val out = Channel<Int>()
    val ja = launch { for (x in a) out.send(x) }
    val jb = launch { for (x in b) out.send(x) }
    launch { ja.join(); jb.join(); out.close() }
    out                                                           // caller gets a channel; see scope caveat
}

(In the merge sketch coroutineScope would wait for the children; in real code take a CoroutineScope receiver and return the channel, as in Q452.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using consumeEach in workers.
  • Expecting results in input order from a worker pool.
  • A worker exception (without a supervisor) cancels sibling workers and loses in-flight jobs (Q461).
  • Pool size equal to Dispatchers.IO cap gives you nothing; bound concurrency deliberately (a Semaphore or limitedParallelism is the alternative, see the shared-state chunk).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you keep ordering? → Single consumer, or shard by key hash into one channel per worker.
  2. Fan-out vs async per item? → Channel fan-out bounds concurrency with N workers and gives backpressure; unbounded async per item can spawn thousands of coroutines.
  3. How do you broadcast the same element to all consumers? → Not a channel feature; use SharedFlow (BroadcastChannel is deprecated).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "multiple coroutines receive from one channel". Senior: FIFO-fair distribution, loses ordering, consumeEach trap, who closes in fan-in, exception handling inside workers, and alternatives for bounded concurrency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A thumbnail generator with 8 workers using consumeEach stopped entirely after the first worker hit a corrupt file.

questions.promptHtml: What do onBufferOverflow and onUndeliveredElement do on Channel(...), and when is each needed?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who only know capacity numbers from those who handle dropped data and resource cleanup.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: onBufferOverflow decides what happens when the buffer is full: SUSPEND (default, backpressure), DROP_OLDEST, or DROP_LATEST. onUndeliveredElement is a callback invoked for every element that was sent but never received: dropped by overflow, rejected because the channel was closed or cancelled, or taken by a receiver that was cancelled before it resumed. I use the callback whenever elements own a resource that needs releasing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Channel<E>(
    capacity = Channel.RENDEZVOUS,
    onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.SUSPEND,
    onUndeliveredElement: ((E) -> Unit)? = null
)
  • SUSPEND: send parks. DROP_OLDEST: removes the head of the buffer, never suspends. DROP_LATEST: discards the element being sent, never suspends. For drop strategies trySend still returns success if the element was accepted into the buffer. A dropped element is reported only via onUndeliveredElement, not via the send result.
  • CONFLATED = capacity 1 + DROP_OLDEST.
  • onUndeliveredElement is called once per undelivered element, synchronously and in an arbitrary context (could be the cancelling thread). Keep it fast, non-blocking, non-throwing; exceptions are wrapped and passed on to the caller or CoroutineExceptionHandler.
  • When the channel is cancel()ed, the callback runs for every element remaining in the buffer.

Elements that are plain data do not need it. Elements that own native memory, Closeable, Bitmap, pooled byte arrays, or an Acknowledgement for a message queue do.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val frames = Channel<Frame>(
    capacity = 4,
    onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST,       // camera: newest frame matters
    onUndeliveredElement = { it.release() }              // return buffer to pool
)

// camera callback thread
fun onFrame(f: Frame) { frames.trySend(f) }              // never blocks; old frame released by callback

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming trySend result tells you about a drop under DROP_OLDEST.
  • Releasing the element twice: once in the callback and once in the consumer after a successful receive. The callback is only for undelivered ones.
  • Doing blocking IO or runBlocking inside the callback.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. DROP_OLDEST vs DROP_LATEST for a sensor? → Usually DROP_OLDEST (freshest data), DROP_LATEST when the first items define the batch.
  2. Does onUndeliveredElement fire after a successful receive? → No; once delivered, ownership is the receiver's.
  3. How do you count drops for metrics? → Increment a counter in onUndeliveredElement (it fires for overflow drops too).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "drops oldest when full". Senior: names the callback for resource cleanup, understands all three trigger conditions, threading caveats, and the ownership boundary of delivered vs undelivered.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A video pipeline leaked pooled buffers on every screen exit until onUndeliveredElement returned them to the pool.

questions.contextHtml:
A junior's PR adds a batch importer. QA reports: "import finishes all 500 rows, but the progress dialog never dismisses and the screen's coroutine count grows by one per import." No crash, no log. Code:

class ImportViewModel(private val repo: Repo) : ViewModel() {
    val done = MutableStateFlow(false)

    fun import(rows: List<Row>) {
        val ch = Channel<Row>(Channel.BUFFERED)
        viewModelScope.launch {
            for (row in rows) ch.send(row)
        }
        viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
            for (row in ch) repo.insert(row)
            done.value = true
        }
    }
}

Red herrings: the DB insert is already main-safe; the buffer size (64) being smaller than the list (500) is not the problem, because the producer just suspends and resumes.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames Room, the dispatcher, or StateFlow not emitting. Or suggests delay or a timeout. They do not notice the producer never closes the channel, so for (row in ch) suspends forever after the last row.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do all 500 rows land in the DB? (yes, so data path works; the hang is after the last element.) Does the problem happen on empty input? Is this a single-consumer pipeline? (yes). That points to end-of-stream signalling.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; ship the one-line fix. If already in production, the leaked consumers die with the ViewModel, so the leak is bounded per screen.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) channel never closed; (b) done.value = true never reached for another reason such as an exception, which would show in logs; (c) dispatcher issue. (a) fits "all rows inserted but nothing after".
  4. How I'd verify each: Run with -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug and dump with DebugProbes, or use the Android Studio coroutine debugger: the consumer is SUSPENDED in ChannelIterator.hasNext. Add a log after the loop; it never prints.
  5. Root cause: hasNext() returns false only when the channel is closed and drained. Nobody calls close(), so the consumer parks forever. Each import leaks one parked coroutine until the ViewModel clears.
  6. Fix: Short term: ch.close() after the producer loop (in a finally, so failure also ends the stream, preferably close(e)). Long term: drop the channel entirely; the example needs no channel at all, a plain loop does the job. If decoupling is wanted, use produce, which closes automatically.
fun import(rows: List<Row>) = viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
    rows.forEach { repo.insert(it) }
    done.value = true
}
// or with a channel:
val ch = produce { rows.forEach { send(it) } }      // auto-closed
for (row in ch) repo.insert(row)
  1. Prevention: Review rule: every hand-made Channel must show who closes it. Prefer produce/channelFlow/flow. A unit test with runTest that asserts completion (a test timeout catches the hang).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a withTimeout to "recover" from the hang since it hides the defect. I would not rely on ViewModel clearing to clean up.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the producer throws midway? → Without close(cause) or produce, same hang; use try/finally with close(e) so the consumer fails fast.
  • What if there are two consumers? → Both hang; close() ends both loops.
  • Could consumeEach have prevented it? → No; it cancels on exit but still waits for close to exit normally.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sync job "worked" in staging where the process died after each run, hiding that the channel was never closed. In production the long-lived process piled up parked coroutines each sync, which showed up weeks later as a slow memory climb.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames dispatcher/Room, adds delays.
  • Hire: identifies the missing close and fixes it.
  • Strong hire: also uses debugger evidence, closes in finally with cause, replaces with produce/simple loop, and states the review rule.

questions.promptHtml: What are trySend, trySendBlocking, and tryReceive? Where would you use each, and what does ChannelResult tell you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Callbacks from non-coroutine code (Java listeners, camera, sensors) cannot call send. The answer shows whether you know how to bridge safely without blocking the main thread.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: trySend never suspends or blocks; it returns a ChannelResult telling me whether the element was accepted. It fails if the buffer is full (and policy is SUSPEND) or the channel is closed. trySendBlocking blocks the calling thread until sent, so it is only for background threads I control. tryReceive is the non-suspending receive. I use trySend inside callbacks and handle the failure case explicitly instead of ignoring it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ChannelResult<T> is an inline value class with three states: success (getOrNull/isSuccess), failed because full/empty (isFailure), closed (isClosed). Helpers: onSuccess {}, onFailure {}, onClosed {}.

When trySend fails:

Channel trySend outcome
RENDEZVOUS with no waiting receiver fails (nobody to hand to)
BUFFERED full, SUSPEND fails
CONFLATED, UNLIMITED, any DROP_* always succeeds while open (drops handled internally)
closed fails with isClosed

trySendBlocking(e) (in kotlinx.coroutines.channels) is basically runBlocking { send(e) } without the event loop: blocks the thread until the send completes; returns a ChannelResult too. Never call it on the main thread (ANR risk) or on a Dispatchers.Default thread you cannot afford to block.

Design rules:

  • Choose a capacity such that trySend failing means something meaningful to you: UNLIMITED (never fails, memory risk), CONFLATED/DROP_* (never fails, may drop), or sized + explicit failure handling.
  • If a callback event must never be lost and the callback is on a thread you control, trySendBlocking gives true backpressure. On a framework thread (Binder, main, camera) it does not.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val events = Channel<SensorSample>(capacity = 32, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)

val listener = object : SensorEventListener {
    override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) {
        events.trySend(SensorSample(e.values[0], e.timestamp))    // never blocks sensor thread
            .onFailure { Metrics.droppedSamples.inc() }           // only closed, with DROP_OLDEST
    }
    override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor?, a: Int) = Unit
}

// background thread you own:
worker.submit { events.trySendBlocking(sample).onClosed { /* stop */ } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• ch.trySend(x) ignoring the result on a RENDEZVOUS channel: silently lost whenever the consumer is busy. This is the #1 "my events disappear" cause.
  • trySendBlocking on main.
  • Treating isFailure and isClosed the same; closed is permanent, full is transient.
  • Calling launch { ch.send(x) } per event inside the callback to avoid failure; unbounded coroutines and lost ordering.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does trySend throw? → Not for full/closed; returns a result. It can throw if onUndeliveredElement throws.
  2. Why prefer trySend + a buffer over runBlocking { send } in a callback? → No thread blocked; the choice of buffer is explicit.
  3. What replaces this boilerplate for listener APIs? → callbackFlow, where trySend is available on ProducerScope (see the callback interop chunk).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "non-suspending send". Senior: tabulates when it fails per capacity, uses ChannelResult handlers, picks capacity first, avoids trySendBlocking on framework threads, and counts drops.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A BLE notification handler used trySend on a rendezvous channel and lost about 15% of notifications whenever the UI was busy; no log, no crash.

questions.promptHtml: What is select in coroutines? Show how you would wait on two channels (or a channel and a timeout) and explain which clause wins when several are ready.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: select is the Go-style multiplexing primitive; the question tests understanding of bias, closed channels and cancellation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: select suspends until the first of several clauses becomes ready and runs only that clause: onReceive, onReceiveCatching, onSend, onAwait, onJoin, onTimeout. Others are discarded without side effects. If several are ready, the first listed wins (it is biased); selectUnbiased picks randomly. On a closed channel onReceive throws, so I use onReceiveCatching.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism: select registers a single waiter on every clause's underlying channel/job. When one fires, the select atomically claims the "selected" state so only one clause completes; the others are unregistered. No element is consumed from a channel whose clause lost, which is the property making it safe to race.

Clauses (all in kotlinx.coroutines.selects):

Clause Source Notes
ch.onReceive { } ReceiveChannel throws if channel closed
ch.onReceiveCatching { result -> } ReceiveChannel gives ChannelResult, handles close
ch.onSend(x) { } SendChannel picks whichever channel can accept
deferred.onAwait { } Deferred
job.onJoin { } Job
onTimeout(ms) { } none @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi

Bias: clause order is priority. If high and low are both ready, high wins. This enables priority queues, but also starvation (Q467).

select is cancellable: cancelling the coroutine cancels the select and unregisters waiters. The clause block runs in the select caller's context after selection.

Flow-era note: for "race two things" I often use select with onAwait, or raceOf-style helpers; for "first of N flows", merge is simpler.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun next(high: ReceiveChannel<Task>, low: ReceiveChannel<Task>): Task? =
    select {
        high.onReceiveCatching { it.getOrNull() }      // listed first = higher priority
        low.onReceiveCatching { it.getOrNull() }
        onTimeout(500) { null }                        // experimental API
    }

suspend fun fastest(a: Deferred<String>, b: Deferred<String>): String =
    select {
        a.onAwait { b.cancel(); it }
        b.onAwait { a.cancel(); it }
    }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• onReceive on a closed channel throws ClosedReceiveChannelException.
  • Looping select over a channel that closed: onReceiveCatching returns closed immediately forever, causing a busy spin. Remove the closed channel from the set.
  • Assuming fairness between clauses.
  • onTimeout in library code without @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is selectUnbiased? → Same as select but shuffles clause order to avoid starvation.
  2. Does a losing onReceive consume an element? → No, only the winning clause consumes.
  3. Use select or Flow merge? → merge for combining streams; select when you need a single decision per iteration with priorities or send/receive mixing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "like Go select". Senior: bias and starvation, the closed-channel spin, onReceiveCatching, atomic claim semantics, experimental status of onTimeout, and when Flow operators are simpler.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A priority dispatcher using select with a hot high-priority channel starved low-priority uploads for hours.

questions.promptHtml: When do you choose a Channel and when a Flow? Give concrete criteria, not "Flow is the modern way".

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The L3 signal is a decision framework with failure modes, not a preference.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Flow is cold, declarative, lifecycle-friendly and multi-collector-safe, so it is my default for data streams. A Channel is hot, point-to-point, and has explicit lifecycle (send, close), so I use it for work queues, one-shot signals, fan-out workers, and as the internal glue behind callbackFlow/channelFlow/buffer/flowOn. For UI I usually expose a Flow (state, or receiveAsFlow of a channel) and keep the Channel private.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Dimension Flow (cold) Channel
Starts on collect on first send, independent of receivers
Multiple consumers each re-runs producer split elements (each element once)
Replay / late subscriber no (cold re-run); StateFlow/SharedFlow add it no, items consumed once; buffered items wait
Lifecycle ends when collector cancels; producer stops you must close/cancel; producer outlives consumers
Backpressure built-in via suspension built-in via capacity
Operators rich (map, combine, debounce...) few, build by hand
Error propagation exception transparency close(cause)
Resource ownership collector owns explicit

Choose Channel when:

  • Work queue / job dispatch with N workers (point-to-point semantics).
  • Handoff where element must be processed exactly once, even if nobody listens now (buffered until a receiver arrives).
  • Coroutines as actors with a mailbox.
  • Bridging a push API into coroutines (usually via callbackFlow, which is a Channel inside). Choose Flow when:
  • Describing a transformation of a stream with operators.
  • Multiple UI consumers need state (StateFlow) or broadcast (SharedFlow).
  • You want the producer to stop automatically when nobody collects.

Interplay: Flow.buffer(), flowOn, produceIn, channelFlow, callbackFlow, and shareIn all use channels internally. receiveAsFlow() / consumeAsFlow() adapt a Channel to a Flow, Flow.produceIn(scope) goes back.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Uploader {
    private val queue = Channel<UploadJob>(Channel.UNLIMITED)    // work queue, private

    fun enqueue(job: UploadJob) { queue.trySend(job) }

    fun start(scope: CoroutineScope) = repeat(3) {
        scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) { for (j in queue) upload(j) }   // exactly-once, 3 workers
    }
}

val clicks: Flow<Unit> = callbackFlow {             // Flow for consumers
    val l = View.OnClickListener { trySend(Unit) }
    view.setOnClickListener(l)
    awaitClose { view.setOnClickListener(null) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a Channel when two screens need the same data: only one gets each element.
  • Using a Flow for a job queue: each collector would re-run the producer or the queue semantics are lost.
  • Exposing Channel publicly instead of Flow/SendChannel.
  • Thinking Flow "replaced" Channel; Flow is built on it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is callbackFlow built on a channel? → Push callbacks need a thread-safe mailbox with trySend, and awaitClose for cleanup.
  2. Channel vs SharedFlow for events? → Channel: exactly one consumer, buffers while absent. SharedFlow: broadcast, drops/never buffers for absent subscribers unless replay.
  3. How would you convert a producer coroutine's Channel into something UI can collect safely? → receiveAsFlow() collected with repeatOnLifecycle, accepting single-consumer semantics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Flow is newer". Senior: gives hot/cold, one-consumer semantics, lifecycle ownership, replay behavior, and knows Flow is implemented with channels.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "shared" Channel of price ticks was collected by two fragments; each saw half the ticks until it moved to SharedFlow.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping app (2.1M DAU, 38% on Android 9 to 11 with aggressive background limits) sends a one-off "navigate to order confirmation" from the ViewModel through a Channel. Crashlytics shows no crash, but support reports "paid, nothing happened, spinner stays". It happens in about 0.4% of payments (~1,100/day). Code:

class CheckoutViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _events = Channel<Event>()               // RENDEZVOUS
    val events = _events.receiveAsFlow()

    fun onPaid(id: String) { _events.trySend(Event.GoToConfirmation(id)) }
}

// Fragment
override fun onViewCreated(v: View, s: Bundle?) {
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
        viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
            vm.events.collect { navigate(it) }
        }
    }
}

Breadcrumbs show the payment webhook returns while the user is in the 3-D Secure bank app (the app is in the background).
questions.promptHtml: Why are events lost, how do you prove it, and what is the right design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use SharedFlow", "use LiveData SingleLiveEvent", or "add replay=1", without explaining which events are lost and why. Or switching to trySend -> send blindly.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the loss correlated with backgrounding / 3-DS / config change? (yes, 3-DS). Is the money state correct on the server? (yes, paid). Is the confirmation reachable from another path (order list)? That sets severity: UX bug, not payment bug.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-driven fallback: on onResume/start, the screen refetches order status; if paid, navigate. Also a banner "Payment received" from push. Ships quickly via remote config.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) trySend on RENDEZVOUS with no active receiver (fragment STOPPED, repeatOnLifecycle cancelled the collector) fails and the event is dropped; (b) event consumed in the window when the view is being destroyed, receive cancelled, element undelivered; (c) process death while in bank app, ViewModel gone; (d) navigation controller not ready. (a) matches "background".
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the ChannelResult of trySend (isFailure) with a Crashlytics custom key; reproduce with developer option "Don't keep activities" plus sending the webhook while backgrounded; Perfetto/logcat to confirm collector cancelled at STOP. For (c), check savedStateHandle and process-death with adb shell am kill.
  5. Root cause: RENDEZVOUS means "needs a receiver now". While the app is STOPPED there is no receiver (the collector is cancelled by repeatOnLifecycle), so trySend fails and the result is ignored. Using send would suspend and deliver on return, but if the process is killed the event is gone anyway. The deeper issue is modeling a navigation as a fire-and-forget event instead of state.
  6. Fix: Short term: use a buffered channel (Channel(Channel.BUFFERED) or UNLIMITED for tiny events) and trySend so the event waits for the next STARTED collector; also handle the failure result. Long term: model it as state: uiState.pendingNavigation: Destination?, which the UI handles then calls vm.onNavigationHandled(), surviving config changes and re-delivery (current Android architecture guidance recommends state-based handling for UI events; I confirm against the current docs before quoting).
private val _events = Channel<Event>(Channel.BUFFERED)
// better: state
data class CheckoutUi(val nav: Destination? = null)
fun onNavHandled() = _ui.update { it.copy(nav = null) }
  1. Prevention: Make the source of truth server-derived, not event-derived; test with Don't keep activities; Crashlytics counter for failed trySend; lint/review rule: never ignore ChannelResult on RENDEZVOUS.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Buffered Channel guarantees delivery within process lifetime to one consumer, but can deliver a stale event after a long background (navigate unexpectedly). State-based has "must acknowledge" boilerplate but no loss/duplicates. I would not use SharedFlow with replay for navigation (replays on every new collector; double navigate).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if two collectors exist? → Each event goes to only one; so state or SharedFlow.
  • What if the event is a snackbar and 10 events pile while backgrounded? → Buffered channel will show 10 snackbars; coalesce or keep only the latest in state.
  • What about process death? → Neither Channel nor state in memory survives; persist or re-derive from server.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added replay=1 to fix lost events and then got double navigation on every rotation; the postmortem moved all one-shot UI into state with explicit acknowledgement.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "just use SharedFlow".
  • Hire: explains rendezvous + trySend failure while STOPPED, fixes with buffer.
  • Strong hire: proposes state-based design, server fallback, instruments ChannelResult, and discusses stale/duplicate delivery trade-offs.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between receiveAsFlow() and consumeAsFlow()? What happens with multiple collectors and when the collector is cancelled?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These two look identical and the wrong choice causes either a dead channel after a config change or an IllegalStateException.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: consumeAsFlow() consumes the channel: it can be collected only once (a second collection throws IllegalStateException), and when that collector finishes or is cancelled, the channel is cancelled too. receiveAsFlow() just receives: it can be collected repeatedly and by multiple collectors (each element still goes to one), and cancelling a collector leaves the channel alive. For UI event flows that must survive resubscription (repeatOnLifecycle), receiveAsFlow() is the one.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Both wrap ReceiveChannel in a Flow, and both are "hot source" flows: collecting does not restart anything. They differ in ownership:

receiveAsFlow() consumeAsFlow()
Collectors many, sequentially or concurrently exactly one, once
Second collect allowed IllegalStateException
Collector cancelled channel stays open channel is cancelled
Concurrent collectors each element delivered to one n/a
Closed channel flow completes flow completes

Consequence for Android: with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED), the collector is cancelled on every STOP and restarted on START. consumeAsFlow() would cancel the channel on the first STOP, then fail or deliver nothing after that. receiveAsFlow() works: elements buffered while stopped are delivered on next START.

Caution: receiveAsFlow() with two active collectors (two fragments, or old-and-new collectors overlapping briefly during restart) splits the stream. The overlap window is small but real; one element can be taken by a collector whose lifecycle is then cancelled, so the element is lost (visible via onUndeliveredElement).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private val _events = Channel<UiEvent>(Channel.BUFFERED)
val events: Flow<UiEvent> = _events.receiveAsFlow()     // survives collector restarts

// DON'T for UI:
val bad: Flow<UiEvent> = _events.consumeAsFlow()
// 1st STOP cancels the channel; later send/receive fail

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• consumeAsFlow() in a ViewModel property read by a Fragment: breaks after the first background/foreground cycle.
  • Thinking receiveAsFlow() is a broadcast.
  • Collecting in both onCreate and onStart code paths so two collectors compete.
  • Using flow.shareIn with a channel flow expecting events to replay.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not StateFlow? → Conflation and equality de-dup swallow repeated identical events; replay of last value redelivers.
  2. How do you avoid losing the in-flight element on cancel? → onUndeliveredElement to requeue, or state-based design.
  3. How do you make the single-consumer rule explicit? → Expose Flow from receiveAsFlow() and document "one collector at a time"; or enforce by a dedicated event-handling base class.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "one of them is single use". Senior: ownership/cancellation semantics for the underlying channel, interaction with repeatOnLifecycle, overlapping-collector splitting, and the undelivered-element race.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team migrated to consumeAsFlow() for tidy code, and after the first app backgrounding no one-shot events were ever delivered again until app restart.

questions.contextHtml:
A photo-backup service (Android foreground service, 4 workers, ~3,000 photos on first sync, p95 upload 1.8 s) uses a channel-based pool. After a release, support sees "sync stops at about 40%, then the notification says 'running' forever". Logs show one java.io.FileNotFoundException (user deleted a photo mid-sync) followed by silence. Code:

suspend fun sync(photos: List<Photo>) = coroutineScope {
    val ch = Channel<Photo>(8)
    launch { photos.forEach { ch.send(it) }; ch.close() }
    repeat(4) {
        launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
            ch.consumeEach { api.upload(it) }          // throws on missing file
        }
    }
}

Red herring: server returns 200 for all uploads in the logs; Wi-Fi is stable.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose the hang, and design the pool so one bad item cannot stall or kill the sync, without leaking resources.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add try/catch around the whole coroutineScope" or "increase workers". Does not see that the failing worker cancels the siblings via the scope and the producer is stuck in send.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should one bad photo fail the whole sync or be skipped and reported? (skip). Are uploads idempotent (retry safe)? Is ordering required? (no). Is the notification tied to scope completion?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix with per-item try/catch that rethrows CancellationException, record failures, continue. Ship as a patch; force a "sync again" for stuck users via remote flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) exception in consumeEach -> consumeEach cancels the channel in its finally block and the exception cancels the coroutineScope; (b) the producer is parked in send on a full buffer (8) while consumers are gone; (c) the cancellation of the scope should unwind the producer, so a hang means something else swallows it: the service uses a different scope that does not rethrow, or the sync call is wrapped in runCatching which swallows the exception and the cancellation, leaving the UI "running". Rank (a)+(c): the failure is real, but notification state is never updated because sync is called inside runCatching.
  4. How I'd verify each: Coroutine debug agent dump (DebugProbes) to see whether workers/producer are alive; log after coroutineScope returns; grep for runCatching around the call; unit test with a fake API failing on item 5 using runTest and a timeout.
  5.
