Root cause: Two defects combine: (1) no per-item failure isolation, so one FileNotFoundException takes down the worker, consumeEach cancels the channel (so the other workers lose their items and the buffered ones are dropped), and the scope fails; (2) the caller swallows the failure with runCatching, so the foreground notification never moves to "failed/finished". The user sees silence.
  6. Fix: Short term: isolate per item, use a plain for, and report results.
suspend fun sync(photos: List<Photo>): SyncReport = coroutineScope {
    val ch = Channel<Photo>(8, onUndeliveredElement = { it.releaseHandle() })
    val failed = Collections.synchronizedList(mutableListOf<Photo>())
    launch { photos.forEach { ch.send(it) }; ch.close() }
    repeat(4) {
        launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
            for (p in ch) {                       // not consumeEach
                try { api.upload(p) }
                catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
                catch (e: Exception) { failed += p; log(e) }
            }
        }
    }
    SyncReport(photos.size - failed.size, failed)   // coroutineScope waits for all children
}

Long term: a persistent queue (WorkManager/Room) with retries per item, so a process kill does not lose position. 7. Prevention: Test with injected failures; lint ban on consumeEach in pools and on runCatching around suspend code without rethrowing cancellation; metrics on per-item failure; a watchdog that fails the sync if no progress for N minutes. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use supervisorScope alone (it would keep the other workers alive but the failing worker still ends and capacity shrinks; per-item catch is cleaner). I would not retry forever in the worker, which would starve the queue behind a poison item.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if one item hangs forever? → Per-item withTimeout; the timeout is a CancellationException subtype, so catch TimeoutCancellationException specifically to count a failure while still propagating real cancellation.
  • 3,000 becomes 300,000 photos? → Do not materialize a list; stream from DB into the channel (produce with paging), keep the buffer small for backpressure.
  • Poison item that crashes workers repeatedly? → Dead-letter list after N attempts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A bulk importer silently stopped at 60% for a minority of users because a single malformed record cancelled a shared consumeEach; the fix was boring per-item isolation plus a "N succeeded, M failed" summary.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: wraps everything in try/catch, adds workers.
  • Hire: spots consumeEach cancelling the channel and fixes per-item handling.
  • Strong hire: also finds the swallowed exception, handles cancellation correctly, uses onUndeliveredElement, discusses persistence and poison items.

questions.promptHtml: How does select work internally, and what are its guarantees and costs? Why can it be unsafe to select over onSend/onReceive with side effects in the clause, and how do you build a "priority queue with timeout" correctly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the atomic-claim mechanism and can reason about priority, starvation, and cancellation, beyond syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: select registers one waiter object with every clause's source. The first source to complete must win an atomic state change on the select instance; losers are then unregistered, and only the winner's clause body runs. That is why a losing onReceive never consumes an element. Clause order is priority, so a priority queue is a select with the high channel first; to avoid starvation I add a fairness policy such as selectUnbiased or a budget. Timeouts via onTimeout (experimental) or by racing a Job.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism, simplified:

select { A.onReceive{..}; B.onReceive{..}; onTimeout(t){..} }
   |
   | 1. try each clause in order: if A has an element right now, claim and return (fast path, no suspension)
   | 2. otherwise register a waiter on A, on B, and a timer
   | 3. suspend
   | 4. first source to fire does CAS(selectState: pending -> selected); losers' CAS fails and they back off
   | 5. unregister all other waiters, then run the winner's block with the produced value

Consequences:

  • Fast path is biased: step 1 checks in listed order, so a continually-ready first clause always wins.
  • Atomic claim means no element is lost to a losing clause. Elements are only taken when the claim succeeds.
  • The winner's block runs after selection; if it throws, the exception propagates out of select.
  • Cancellation: cancelling the caller while suspended unregisters waiters; no element consumed.
  • Cost: registering N waiters per call; do not select over thousands of channels in a hot loop. Merging into one channel (fan-in) is cheaper.
  • Version note: select, onReceive, onReceiveCatching, onSend, onAwait, onJoin are stable; onTimeout is experimental at time of writing (check the KDoc/CHANGES for your version). The select internals were reworked alongside the channel rewrite in the 1.7 line (new SelectClause interfaces), so do not depend on internal classes.

Priority + fairness pattern: serve high first, but after K consecutive high items let one low through; or use selectUnbiased and accept probabilistic priority.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun loop(high: ReceiveChannel<Task>, low: ReceiveChannel<Task>) {
    var streak = 0
    while (true) {
        val t: Task? = if (streak >= 8) {                       // fairness budget
            streak = 0
            select {
                low.onReceiveCatching { it.getOrNull() }
                high.onReceiveCatching { it.getOrNull() }
            }
        } else {
            select {
                high.onReceiveCatching { streak++; it.getOrNull() }
                low.onReceiveCatching { streak = 0; it.getOrNull() }
            }
        }
        if (t == null) return                                   // closed
        run(t)
    }
}

(When one channel closes while the other has data, the loop above returns early; production code should track which closed and drop it from the set.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Closed channel in a select loop returns immediately forever (CPU spin).
  • Side effects before select (like ch.send in the clause expression) are executed even for the losing clauses; the argument to onSend(x) is evaluated eagerly.
  • Using select where merge/combine of flows reads better.
  • Treating onTimeout as a stable API in a shared library.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does "biased" buy you? → Deterministic priority and a cheap fast path; cost is starvation.
  2. How do you select across a dynamic number of channels? → Not directly; fan-in into one channel, or build the select with a loop over a list inside the select lambda (the builder lambda can register clauses in a loop).
  3. Why not poll with tryReceive in a loop? → Busy-waiting; select suspends until something is ready.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: syntax and examples. Senior: atomic claim, fast-path bias and its starvation consequence, closed-channel spin, eager argument evaluation of onSend, cost vs fan-in, and API stability caveats.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A job scheduler's low-priority queue stalled for hours under steady high-priority load until a streak budget was added.

questions.contextHtml:
A fitness app streams accelerometer data at 100 Hz from a wearable over BLE, writes to Room in batches, and also feeds a live chart. Android vitals shows OOM-kill rate rising from 0.2% to 1.9% of sessions after launching "workout recording" to all users, concentrated on 2-3 GB RAM devices, in sessions longer than 40 minutes. Heap dumps show ~14M Sample objects retained by a LinkedQueue inside a channel. Code:

private val samples = Channel<Sample>(Channel.UNLIMITED)
fun onBleNotification(s: Sample) { samples.trySend(s) }           // 100 Hz x 3 sensors

scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
    samples.consumeAsFlow().chunked(500).collect { db.insertAll(it) }   // ~1.2 s per batch under contention
}

(chunked here is a custom Flow operator.) Red herrings: the chart collector is cheap; GC logs show no leak after sessions end.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the growth, estimate it, and fix it without losing the data that matters.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap (largeHeap)" or "clear the channel sometimes". Does not compute arrival vs service rate or choose a capacity policy per consumer.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must every sample be persisted, or only the chart can be lossy? What is the data rate and the DB write throughput? What happens if the DB is slow (disk contention, background sync)? Which devices?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature flag to cap recording length or reduce sample rate to 50 Hz; ship a bounded buffer with drop metrics as a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) arrival rate exceeds service rate for sustained periods, and UNLIMITED hides it by growing; (b) per-sample object overhead is large; (c) consumeAsFlow collector stalled by DB lock; (d) leaked collector. GC logs showing clean after the session say (d) is out.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute rates: 100 Hz x 3 sensors = 300 samples/s arrive. DB handles 500 per 1.2 s = ~417/s nominal, but under contention 1.2 s can go to 3+ s per batch = ~160/s. Deficit of ~140/s: after 40 min (2,400 s) that is ~336k backlog. The observed 14M implies the consumer was stalled for far longer, or rate is higher; the profiler memory view and a counter of channel size (my own AtomicInteger inc/dec) confirm. Check Sample size: object header 12-16 B + 3 floats 12 B + long 8 B + references ~ 40 B per sample, so 14M x 40 B = 560 MB, exceeding a 256-512 MB per-app heap limit on those devices. Math matches the OOM.
  5. Root cause: UNLIMITED removes backpressure. With arrival > service for any sustained period, backlog grows linearly until the heap limit. There is no signal to the producer, and the OOM arrives long after the slowdown began.
  6. Fix: Short term: bounded buffer with explicit policy. Long term: split the stream by requirement.
// Persistence: lossless but bounded, apply backpressure to the BLE side by batching on the producer thread
private val persist = Channel<Sample>(capacity = 2_000, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.SUSPEND)
// BLE callback runs on a thread we own: block that thread (not main/binder) if the DB cannot keep up
fun onBleNotification(s: Sample) { persist.trySendBlocking(s).onClosed { stop() } }

// Chart: lossy is fine
private val live = Channel<Sample>(capacity = 256, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)

Further: larger DB batches (insertAll 2,000 rows in one transaction), WAL mode, and storing samples as a primitive float array ring buffer instead of objects. If still behind, spill to a file append-log and import later. 7. Prevention: Gauge metric "queue depth"; alert when above 50% capacity; soak test 2 hours with throttled DB; never use UNLIMITED across a rate boundary without a documented bound. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: largeHeap only delays the OOM. Dropping persistence samples silently corrupts the workout; blocking the BLE thread may cause BLE stack drops if it blocks too long, so the buffer must be sized for the worst DB stall, e.g. 2,000 samples = 6.7 s at 300/s (math: 2,000/300).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the BLE callback is on the main thread? → Never block; use a larger drop-aware or off-heap ring buffer and count drops.
  • Why not Flow.buffer(UNLIMITED)? → Same memory problem hidden in the operator.
  • 10x devices at 1 kHz? → Down-sample/aggregate at the source, batch on device, write binary segments, not rows.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A telemetry pipeline "never lost data" thanks to an unlimited queue and then took out its own process under a flaky disk; after the fix it dropped the newest chart points deliberately and kept every persisted sample.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases heap, ignores rate math.
  • Hire: bounded channel with a sensible overflow policy.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the backlog, splits persistence vs live paths, picks blocking vs dropping per thread ownership, adds metrics and soak tests.

questions.contextHtml: You own the "outbox" of a chat app (20M MAU). Users send messages offline; the app must deliver in order per conversation, retry with backoff, and never double-send. Today each send does scope.launch { api.send(msg) }, causing out-of-order delivery under flaky networks (roughly 0.8% of chats see reordering) and duplicates on retry. A teammate proposes "one Channel for everything with one consumer coroutine". Another proposes a Channel per conversation.
questions.promptHtml: Design it, and defend the choice between one global channel, per-conversation channels, and a persistent queue.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks a single channel and one consumer because "it keeps order" without noting head-of-line blocking across conversations, process death loss, or idempotency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is ordering required globally or per conversation (per conversation)? Is the server idempotent by client message id? Must unsent messages survive process death (yes)? Max messages per conversation in the queue?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a client-generated UUID per message and server-side de-dup, which stops duplicates today regardless of the queue design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: the choice among designs: (a) global channel: simple, preserves global order, but a slow/failed conversation blocks everyone (head-of-line); (b) per-conversation channel with one consumer each: order within a conversation, parallel across, but unbounded number of coroutines/channels and they die with the process; (c) persisted outbox in Room + per-conversation worker driven by a channel only as a wake-up signal: survives restarts.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test with 1,000 active conversations, one at 100% failure; measure delivery latency percentiles of the healthy ones. Kill process mid-send and verify no loss/dup. Fake server with random 5xx/timeouts, test-run with runTest virtual time for backoff.
  5. Root cause (of today's issue): Independent launch per message with no serialization key: retries race with later sends and the first-to-arrive wins.
  6. Fix: Room table outbox(id, conversationId, seq, payload, state, attempts). A Channel<ConversationId>(Channel.UNLIMITED) (tiny elements, bounded by conversation count after de-dup) is only a wake-up. A coordinator keeps Map<ConversationId, Job> and ensures at most one active sender per conversation (actor-like), which loops: take next row by seq, send with the message UUID, mark delivered or backoff on failure.
class Outbox(private val dao: OutboxDao, private val api: Api, private val scope: CoroutineScope) {
    private val wake = Channel<ConversationId>(Channel.UNLIMITED)
    private val active = HashMap<ConversationId, Job>()          // touched only by the coordinator

    init {
        scope.launch {                                           // single coordinator coroutine = confinement
            for (cid in wake) {
                if (active[cid]?.isActive == true) continue
                active[cid] = launch { drain(cid) }
            }
        }
    }
    fun enqueue(m: Msg) { scope.launch { dao.insert(m); wake.send(m.conversationId) } }

    private suspend fun drain(cid: ConversationId) {
        while (true) {
            val m = dao.nextPending(cid) ?: return
            try { api.send(m.id, m.payload); dao.markSent(m.id) }
            catch (e: IOException) { delay(backoff(m.attempts)); dao.bumpAttempts(m.id) }
        }
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Idempotency key tests; chaos tests with random kills; metric on queue age; cap attempts with dead-letter state shown to user.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make the channel the source of truth (lost on process death). I would not use a global single consumer (head-of-line). If per-conversation order is the only requirement, a pure WorkManager unique-work chain per conversation (beginUniqueWork + APPEND) may be even less code; the channel solution gives finer control over backoff and foreground latency. In-process the "actor" is just a coroutine owning a channel (the old actor builder is marked obsolete, so I build it by hand).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The app is killed mid-request and the server got it? → Idempotency key makes the retry safe; the row stays pending until acked.
  • 50k queued conversations? → Don't keep a Job per idle conversation; spawn per wake, finish when empty (as above).
  • Why not Mutex per conversation? → Works for in-memory serialization, but queue + persistence is still needed for retries and restarts; a channel gives backpressure and a visible queue.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A support spike of "messages arrive out of order" was fixed not by the channel but by the client message ID plus a per-conversation sequence number the server enforced.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: single channel, says "channels are ordered".
  • Hire: per-key serialization, idempotency key, backoff.
  • Strong hire: persistent outbox, channel as wake signal, confinement/actor reasoning, head-of-line analysis, WorkManager comparison, load/chaos tests.

questions.promptHtml: How is Channel implemented under the hood, and which channel-related APIs are obsolete (BroadcastChannel, actor, ConflatedBroadcastChannel, receiveOrNull)? What replaced them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors are expected to avoid deprecated APIs and understand performance characteristics of the primitive they rely on.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Modern Channel is a lock-free, segment-based structure: an (conceptually) infinite array of cells split into fixed-size linked segments, with atomic counters for send and receive positions. Senders and receivers each take a cell index, then either hand off, buffer, or park a continuation in the cell. That implementation replaced the older linked-list one around kotlinx.coroutines 1.7. BroadcastChannel and ConflatedBroadcastChannel are deprecated in favor of SharedFlow/StateFlow; receiveOrNull is replaced by receiveCatching; the actor builder is marked obsolete (build it with launch + channel).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Implementation sketch (from the published design by the library authors; I describe it in my own words):

  • Two monotonically increasing counters: sendersCounter and receiversCounter. A send does fetch-and-add on its counter to claim cell i; a receive does the same on its counter.
  • Cells live in segments (default segment size is small, e.g. 32 cells), linked into a list. Old segments become garbage as both counters pass them.
  • Per cell state machine: empty -> element stored (sender first) -> element taken; or empty -> waiter registered (receiver first) -> rendezvous/resume. Buffered channels let a sender complete without a waiter when i < receivers + capacity.
  • Result: no global lock, a few atomic ops per operation, good scalability under contention, and less allocation than the old node-per-element list. Version note: the new implementation arrived in the 1.7.0 line; before that, rendezvous/buffered channels were separate classes (array-based and linked-list-based). I do not quote exact segment sizes as stable since they are internal.

Obsolete / replaced APIs:

Old Status Use instead
BroadcastChannel deprecated MutableSharedFlow
ConflatedBroadcastChannel deprecated MutableStateFlow
broadcast {} builder / broadcastIn deprecated shareIn / stateIn
receiveOrNull() removed/deprecated receiveCatching()
poll() / offer() removed/deprecated tryReceive() / trySend()
actor {} @ObsoleteCoroutinesApi launch + Channel
isEmpty/isFull/isClosedForSend delicate design without them
(Exact deprecation level — warning vs error vs hidden — differs by version; check the CHANGES.md of the version you use.)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// actor replacement
class Counter(scope: CoroutineScope) {
    private sealed interface Msg
    private object Inc : Msg
    private class Get(val reply: CompletableDeferred<Int>) : Msg
    private val inbox = Channel<Msg>(Channel.UNLIMITED)
    init {
        scope.launch {
            var n = 0                                  // confined to this coroutine
            for (m in inbox) when (m) {
                Inc -> n++
                is Get -> m.reply.complete(n)
            }
        }
    }
    fun inc() { inbox.trySend(Inc) }
    suspend fun get(): Int = CompletableDeferred<Int>().also { inbox.send(Get(it)) }.await()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Copying old blog posts using BroadcastChannel, offer, poll, receiveOrNull.
  • Claiming "channels use locks" or "use a ConcurrentLinkedQueue". They are lock-free.
  • Believing actor was removed; it is obsolete, not necessarily gone; check the version.
  • Quoting an internal segment size as API.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a segment list, not a ring buffer? → Unbounded and elastic capacity without resizing; old segments are freed once passed.
  2. Why did broadcast channels go away? → SharedFlow/StateFlow cover them with clearer semantics, replay, and better lifecycle integration.
  3. How does a parked receiver get resumed? → The sender finds the registered continuation in the cell, CAS-es it to completed, and resumes it via its dispatcher.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "BroadcastChannel is deprecated". Senior: describes counter-and-cell design, why it scales, and migration mappings, with explicit uncertainty about version details.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A library upgrade to the 1.7+ line changed timing characteristics of an app that relied on accidental ordering between two channels, exposing a latent race.

questions.contextHtml:
In a ride-hailing app, a LocationRepository exposes val updates: ReceiveChannel<Location> produced from GPS. The map screen and the ETA service both do for (loc in repo.updates) .... In QA the map "jitters" and the ETA is often stale. Telemetry shows each consumer receives about half of the points (map gets 1 Hz out of 2 Hz).

class LocationRepository(scope: CoroutineScope) {
    val updates: ReceiveChannel<Location> = scope.produce(capacity = Channel.CONFLATED) {
        gps.requests().collect { send(it) }
    }
}

Red herring: GPS provider interval is stable at 500 ms.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, why does it split points, and what would you ship?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "GPS is unreliable" or "increase capacity". Fails to recognize point-to-point semantics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do both consumers need every point or just the latest? Should GPS run when nobody listens? Late subscriber needs the last known location?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make each consumer read from its own source or share via SharedFlow quickly; as a stopgap give the ETA service a repo.latest copy kept in a @Volatile var.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) point-to-point delivery: each element goes to one receiver; (b) conflation drops points, but that would hit both consumers, not a clean 50/50 split; (c) dispatcher thrash. The even split points to (a).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log element ids per consumer; count; two consumers both increments; unit test with runTest and two collectors on one channel.
  5. Root cause: A Channel hands each element to exactly one waiting receiver, in FIFO order of waiting. Two receivers alternate, so each sees every other point. Also, consumeEach/cancel by one consumer would stop the other.
  6. Fix: Use a hot broadcast primitive that reflects the semantics: location is state, so a StateFlow (or SharedFlow(replay=1)) shared with WhileSubscribed.
class LocationRepository(scope: CoroutineScope) {
    val updates: StateFlow<Location?> = gps.requests()
        .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null)
}
  1. Prevention: Never expose ReceiveChannel from a repository with more than one potential consumer; code-review checklist item "how many consumers?"; test with two collectors.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not BroadcastChannel (deprecated). Not duplicating the GPS request per consumer (battery). StateFlow conflates, which is right for position; if the ETA needs every point (distance integration), use SharedFlow(replay=0, extraBufferCapacity=...) and size it for its slowest consumer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• ETA needs every point, map only the latest? → One SharedFlow; the map uses conflate().
  • What if I want fan-out on purpose (process each point exactly once)? → Then a Channel is right: that is a work queue, not a state stream.
  • How do I stop GPS when nobody watches? → WhileSubscribed cancels the upstream.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team debugged "half the pings" for two days believing the sensor was flaky; the repository had quietly gained a second reader.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames hardware/capacity.
  • Hire: identifies point-to-point delivery and moves to SharedFlow/StateFlow.
  • Strong hire: chooses StateFlow vs SharedFlow by semantics, accounts for battery via WhileSubscribed, and writes a two-collector test.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review: a notification service in an Android foreground process (also running on a small gateway) multiplexes three channels in one select loop: critical (alerts), normal (messages), and bulk (marketing/analytics uploads). On a promo day the bulk queue grew to 180k items, the oldest 9 hours, while the CPU stayed at ~20%. Critical and normal channels were emitting about 40 items/s combined, always ready. Dashboard: "bulk delivery latency p99 = 9 h, no errors". Code:

while (isActive) {
    select<Unit> {
        critical.onReceive { send(it) }
        normal.onReceive   { send(it) }
        bulk.onReceive     { send(it) }
    }
}

Red herring: the sender coroutine send(it) takes ~5 ms (200 items/s max capacity).
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what happened, why was it invisible, and how do you fix and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale up the workers" (CPU is idle) or "add more channels". Misses that biased select starves lower-priority clauses only if higher ones are always ready, and that capacity existed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is bulk allowed to wait forever, or is there an SLA (e.g. 15 min)? What is the capacity of the downstream sender? Are critical and normal ever idle?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drain bulk with a separate temporary worker rate-limited to the downstream's spare capacity (200/s capacity minus 40/s used = 160/s spare, drains 180k in about 19 minutes: 180,000/160 = 1,125 s).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) bias: select checks clauses in order; with critical/normal frequently ready, bulk is hit only when both are empty; (b) downstream saturation; (c) bulk channel closed/stalled; (d) dispatcher starvation. Data: average load is 40 of 200 items/s, so on average critical/normal should be empty 80% of the time and pure steady-state bias cannot explain a 9-hour tail. That pushes me to burstiness (see next step) rather than (b) or (d).
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure per-clause selection counts. Looking deeper: the send(it) is 5 ms; during this time critical/normal accumulate; in bursts, they refill faster than the loop returns, i.e. promo traffic arrives as bursts of 100s, during which bulk is blocked, then it gets some chance. Check arrival patterns via histograms; if critical/normal inter-arrival is below 5 ms in bursts, the loop never reaches bulk during bursts. I verify with a fake load generator replicating burst traces in runTest and counting selections.
  5. Root cause: Biased select + bursty higher-priority arrivals + no aging. Bulk was served only in gaps; the gaps were short or rare under the promo's bursty profile, and no metric showed per-queue age, only errors. The "no errors" dashboard hid a latency SLO violation.
  6. Fix: Short term: weighted fairness. Long term: aging plus per-class rate limits.
var streak = 0
while (isActive) {
    val item: Msg? = select {
        if (streak < 8) {                                      // bounded priority
            critical.onReceiveCatching { streak++; it.getOrNull() }
            normal.onReceiveCatching   { streak++; it.getOrNull() }
        }
        bulk.onReceiveCatching { streak = 0; it.getOrNull() }
        if (streak >= 8) { critical.onReceiveCatching { streak = 0; it.getOrNull() } }
    }
    item?.let { send(it) }
}

(Simplified sketch: clauses can be registered conditionally inside the select builder; handle closed channels by dropping them from the set.) Alternative: run three consumers sharing a rate limiter (a token bucket or Semaphore(n) for concurrency) so bulk has its own lane at reduced priority. 7. Prevention: SLO metrics on oldest-item age per queue; alert at age thresholds, not error counts; load test with burst traces; review rule: "priority needs a starvation bound". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: selectUnbiased alone gives probabilistic fairness but loses priority for critical alerts. Separate lanes isolate classes best but need capacity planning (and keep critical lane reserved). I would not blindly increase worker count since the downstream is the real limit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if bulk must never delay critical by more than 100 ms? → Dedicated critical lane (own coroutine and downstream capacity); bulk gets leftover.
  • What if a queue closes? → Remove it from the set to avoid the closed-channel spin.
  • How would Flow express this? → merge loses priority; a custom operator or separate collectors with a shared limiter is closer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The team had a gold-plated priority scheme, and a dashboard that only graphed throughput and error rate; the 9-hour tail was found by a support ticket, not by monitoring.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale-out / "add CPU".
  • Hire: identifies biased select starvation and adds a fairness bound.
  • Strong hire: separates mean capacity from burst behavior, quantifies drain time, adds age-based SLO metrics, and chooses lanes vs weighted select with trade-offs.
